unit.summary: Understand UIKit and SwiftUI ownership, build safe navigation and asynchronous UI, test at the right boundary, and trace active features end to end.

lessons.title: UIKit: lifecycle, layout, and who owns a screen
lessons.summary: Build a precise model of UIViewController appearance, UIKit containment, layout, and ARC ownership without assuming Android lifecycle equivalence.
objectives: Distinguish controller lifetime, view loading, appearance, and scene activity.
Build a small UIKit screen using actions and Auto Layout.
Draw strong and weak ownership edges for a controller, model, and delegate.
Embed a hosted screen using the full child-controller containment sequence.

sections.title: A familiar screen, a different ownership system
sections.html:
Imagine an Android Fragment containing a title, a form, and a Continue button. You already separate rendering, navigation, and business state; the new work is understanding the objects that carry those responsibilities. UIKit is Apple's imperative interface framework. A UIView is a reference-type object that participates in a view hierarchy and renders or receives input. A UIViewController manages a root view and coordinates its presentation, interactions, and child controllers. Neither is an Activity. A controller has useful similarities to a Fragment, but the callback contracts and restoration rules differ.

A UIWindow displays a hierarchy within a window scene. A navigation controller is a container that manages a stack of controllers. A view controller owns its root view; a view owns its subviews. A navigation controller retains the controllers on its stack. These ownership relationships explain why a screen can remain alive after it stops being visible. UIKit does not install an Android ViewModelStore for every controller or automatically cancel its asynchronous jobs.

Start every investigation with four questions: who constructs the controller, who retains it, who supplies its model, and which event makes the flow finish? In this checkout, a small SwiftUI demo can construct a UIKit controller through a representable wrapper, while the real feature retains its model elsewhere. The same visual screen can therefore have different ownership boundaries in a demo and in production.

sections.title: Loading, appearing, disappearing, and deallocation
sections.html:
Controller initialization creates the object and establishes dependencies. Accessing view can load its root view even when no pixels are visible; loadViewIfNeeded() makes that intent explicit. loadView() creates the root hierarchy. Override it for a fully custom root view, or use the default implementation and configure subviews in viewDidLoad(). Do not call super.loadView() when your override supplies its own root view. viewDidLoad() is a setup event for the loaded hierarchy, not a guarantee that navigation or window geometry is ready.

viewWillAppear(_:) occurs around an appearance transition, and viewDidAppear(_:) after appearance completes. They can run repeatedly: push a detail, pop back, and the original controller appears again. viewIsAppearing(_:) is a newer callback useful when updated traits and geometry are available during appearance; check the target's SDK and deployment support before adopting it. Layout callbacks, including viewDidLayoutSubviews(), can run many times independently of creation or fetching.

viewDidDisappear(_:) says the view disappeared; it does not prove that the flow was cancelled, the controller was popped, or ARC deallocated it. A presented screen may cover it, and navigation transitions may be interactive. Read the container's removal or dismissal evidence before reporting a terminal result. deinit means an instance is being deallocated; relying on it for timely cancellation is dangerous when a task retains the owner. Scene activation and backgrounding are separate from controller appearance. Choose setup, refresh, and cleanup events according to the product behavior, not by matching callback names to onResume.

sections.title: Read a UIKit implementation line by line
sections.html:
The following synthetic example belongs in an iOS UIKit target. import UIKit makes framework types available. @MainActor marks UI access as isolated to the main actor. final prevents subclassing; : UIViewController names the superclass. override replaces inherited behavior, and calling super preserves framework behavior. An instance property survives repeated appearances because the controller remains the same object.

import UIKit

@MainActor
final class CounterController: UIViewController {
    private let titleLabel = UILabel()
    private var tapCount = 0

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()
        view.backgroundColor = .systemBackground
        titleLabel.numberOfLines = 0

        let button = UIButton(type: .system)
        button.setTitle("Add one", for: .normal)
        button.addAction(UIAction { [weak self] _ in
            guard let self else { return }
            self.tapCount += 1
            self.render()
        }, for: .touchUpInside)

        let stack = UIStackView(arrangedSubviews: [titleLabel, button])
        stack.axis = .vertical
        stack.spacing = 16
        stack.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false
        view.addSubview(stack)
        let safe = view.safeAreaLayoutGuide
        NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
            stack.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: safe.topAnchor, constant: 24),
            stack.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: safe.leadingAnchor, constant: 16),
            stack.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: safe.trailingAnchor, constant: -16)
        ])
        render()
    }

    private func render() {
        titleLabel.text = "Count: \(tapCount)"
    }
}

UIAction wraps an event closure; _ discards its action parameter. The capture list [weak self] makes the controller reference optional and non-owning. guard let self else unwraps it for the closure's remaining scope. .touchUpInside, .vertical, and .systemBackground omit type names because the surrounding APIs establish their types. String interpolation, \(tapCount), inserts a value. The action mutates state and then renders explicitly, unlike a declarative state observation system.

sections.title: Ownership diagrams explain more than callback logs
sections.html:
ARC counts strong references rather than tracing an arbitrary object graph like the Java garbage collector. A class property is strong unless declared otherwise. Suppose controller A strongly holds model B, while B strongly holds an event closure that captures A. A → B → closure → A is a cycle; removing A from a navigation stack does not break it. A weak capture can remove that last ownership edge, but it must preserve the intended lifetime of the operation. Ask whether the callback should still occur if the screen owner has disappeared.

Delegation is common in this repository. A delegate protocol constrained with : AnyObject allows only class conformers, which makes a weak var delegate: SomeDelegate? possible. ? permits the reference to become nil after deallocation. The caller must retain the delegate somewhere else. Assigning a newly created delegate directly into a weak property can make it vanish immediately. The address-form demo retains its coordinator in state, then assigns it as the model's weak delegate.

Weak is an ownership decision, not an optimization you apply to every property. The parent normally retains children, and a flow owner normally retains a coordinator until a result arrives. A task closure can retain a controller across an await. Unwrapping a weak capture into a strong local before suspension deliberately extends that lifetime until the operation finishes. This may be correct; it is not proof of a permanent leak. Document the lifetime you want, and give long-running tasks an explicit stop or finish path. Unit 3 develops the concurrency details.

sections.title: Constraints, safe areas, and repeatable rendering
sections.html:
Auto Layout is a system of constraints between attributes such as leading edges, heights, and baselines. Turning translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints off tells UIKit not to derive competing constraints from the legacy resizing mask. NSLayoutConstraint.activate enables the array of constraints. Negative trailing constants inset the trailing edge. The safe-area guide avoids areas obscured by system or container UI; it is not equivalent to applying the same padding to every device.

A vertical UIStackView arranges its arranged subviews and uses their intrinsic sizes. The label and button in the example provide intrinsic height, so top and horizontal constraints are enough for that small demonstration. Larger forms need scroll behavior and a complete sizing strategy. Hard-coded frame dimensions inside viewDidLoad() are fragile because the eventual container size may differ. Do geometry-dependent work in layout callbacks or constraints, and avoid adding the same subviews or constraints repeatedly there.

Rendering should be repeatable: applying the same state twice should yield the same visible result without starting another request or registering another action. That principle is familiar from Android rendering functions. In UIKit it must be enforced explicitly. For keyboard and first-responder problems, inspect unnecessary rebuilding as well as layout. The production address form guards identical error writes because redundant observed changes can disturb its hosted input UI. Treat that as a concrete example of why identity and no-op updates matter.

sections.title: A child controller is more than its root view
sections.html:
When UIKit contains another controller, establish both the controller relationship and the view relationship. Merely calling addSubview(child.view) does not establish controller containment. Apple uses the controller tree to route appearance, traits, and other system behavior. UIHostingController is a UIKit controller whose content is SwiftUI; it obeys the same containment rule.

import SwiftUI
import UIKit

@MainActor
func embedMessage(in parent: UIViewController) -> UIViewController {
    let child = UIHostingController(rootView: Text("Synthetic demo"))
    parent.addChild(child)
    child.view.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false
    parent.view.addSubview(child.view)
    NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
        child.view.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: parent.view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.topAnchor),
        child.view.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: parent.view.leadingAnchor),
        child.view.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: parent.view.trailingAnchor),
        child.view.bottomAnchor.constraint(equalTo: parent.view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.bottomAnchor)
    ])
    child.didMove(toParent: parent)
    return child
}

in is an external argument label here: call embedMessage(in: controller), while the function body uses parent. addChild performs the incoming willMove notification. After installing the view and constraints, call didMove(toParent:). Removal reverses the relationship: call willMove(toParent: nil), remove the root view and any separately managed constraints, then removeFromParent(), which sends the outgoing completion. The booking address form's bind() factory returns a hosted controller and explicitly leaves containment to its caller.

sections.title: Trace the demo without inventing production behavior
sections.html:
Open ContentView and follow the Member ID entry into MemberIdDemo. Its UIKit destination uses MemberIdUIKitDemo, a SwiftUI wrapper that constructs a plain controller with three member-ID states. The state array is synthetic presentation data; constructing this controller does not fetch an insurance record. Notice the project uses SnapKit's snp.makeConstraints and local fluent helpers such as with(axis:). Those are dependency or repository APIs, not Swift or UIKit language features.

Compare that static controller with the visit-reason host. It waits for viewDidAppear, checks that a navigation controller exists, retains the flow coordinator, and then starts it. This is evidence for its integration strategy, not a universal rule that every network request belongs in viewDidAppear. Its retained-coordinator guard prevents repeated starts as appearance callbacks recur.

For a useful debugging notebook, record object identities, appearance events, parent/container changes, and task start/finish separately. Ask what a push, pop, modal presentation, and cancelled interactive gesture should do. A refresh on every appearance might be desirable for a volatile list and destructive for an unsaved form. Once you can explain those choices, UIKit stops feeling like a renamed Android lifecycle and becomes a system with explicit, testable ownership decisions.

quiz.question: A controller's view disappears when a detail screen is pushed. What can you conclude?
options: The controller has been deallocated.
Its view disappeared; its owner may still retain the controller.
All tasks owned by the controller were cancelled.
quiz.explanation: Appearance describes visibility transitions. The navigation stack may retain the controller, and UIKit does not automatically cancel tasks stored by it.

quiz.question: A model has a weak delegate. What must the caller arrange?
options: Retain the delegate elsewhere for the intended callback lifetime.
Use unowned for every reference back to the controller.
Create a new delegate before every render.
quiz.explanation: Weak references do not keep objects alive. A controller or another explicit owner must strongly retain the delegate; unowned risks accessing a deallocated object.

quiz.question: Which operation is required after installing a child controller's view and constraints?
options: Call the child's viewDidLoad() manually.
Only retain child.view.
Call child.didMove(toParent: parent) after parent.addChild(child).
quiz.explanation: The complete containment sequence installs the parent-child controller relationship and sends its completion. UIKit owns lifecycle dispatch; calling viewDidLoad yourself bypasses that contract.

exercise.brief: In a separate learner scratch iOS target, build the synthetic counter and explain its lifetime through push, cover, pop, and release. Do not edit the client checkout.
steps: Create CounterController using the example and present it from a UINavigationController.
Add diagnostic breakpoint actions to viewDidLoad, viewDidAppear, viewDidDisappear, and deinit; record events separately from state changes.
Increment twice, push a blank detail, then pop back. Explain why the count remains two.
Draw ownership arrows for navigation controller → counter → view hierarchy → button → action. Mark the weak closure edge.
Embed a small hosting controller using the full containment sequence, then remove it correctly.
acceptance: The counter remains two after returning from detail.
Constraints adapt to the container's safe area without duplicate installation.
The ownership drawing explains why disappearing does not imply deallocation.
The child controller receives containment completion and is removable without orphaning its view.
exercise.solution:
The count lives on the controller, and the navigation stack retains that same controller while the detail is visible. Therefore the return path should not rerun one-time hierarchy construction or reset the count. A diagnostic log may show multiple appearance events with one initial load. After popping the counter itself, release any scratch variables that also retained it before expecting deinit.

The action has a weak reference to the counter; the button and action therefore do not keep the controller alive through a strong reference cycle. A temporarily promoted self remains alive during the synchronous event, which is what the render requires. The parent retains its hosted child through containment. To remove that child, use the following sequence in a main-actor UI context:

child.willMove(toParent: nil)
child.view.removeFromSuperview()
child.removeFromParent()

Here child is the hosted controller retained by your scratch owner. If you retain it in a separate property, clear that property as part of the owner's removal policy. Do not force a deallocation conclusion from a visibility log: first audit every remaining strong reference. The worked answer is a design and inspection guide; this course author has not built or run your scratch app.

lessons.title: SwiftUI: state, bindings, identity, and Observation
lessons.summary: Choose the owner of each value, understand SwiftUI's descriptive View values, and distinguish Observation from persistence and lifecycle management.
objectives: Explain why a SwiftUI View value is not an Android View object.
Choose among plain properties, State, Binding, Bindable, and legacy object wrappers.
Explain how view identity governs state storage and why Observation does not persist data.
Read the address-form demo's modern state flow alongside the member-ID demo's legacy observation.

sections.title: Use your Compose experience, then check the boundary
sections.html:
In Compose, a composable describes UI from state and can run many times. That experience is useful when reading SwiftUI. A SwiftUI View commonly is a small struct value that describes an interface; it is not a mutable Android View, and it is not the long-lived UIKit view object that eventually displays it. SwiftUI evaluates descriptions, tracks dependencies and identity, and reconciles the rendered hierarchy. Creating a new description does not necessarily create a new screen or lose its state.

The declaration struct Editor: View means the value type conforms to the View protocol. Its var body: some View is a computed property returning a particular view type that the caller need not spell out. some is an opaque return type: the compiler still knows the concrete type, so it differs from unrestricted dynamic interface boxing. Containers use result-builder syntax to combine expressions such as Text and Button without manually constructing a list of children.

Keep body focused on describing current state. A request inside it can run again when a dependency changes; a model initialized there can be recreated. Rendering callbacks and value initializers are not a durable screen-creation signal. Organize work around an explicit owner and events such as an action or a view-associated task, which session 011 will explain.

sections.title: State is storage associated with identity
sections.html:
@State is a property wrapper used to connect a declaration to storage managed by SwiftUI. The wrapper's value syntax looks like an ordinary variable, but SwiftUI maintains the state for that view identity across repeated description creation. Keep local state private so the implementation remains its clear owner. This resembles Compose's remembered state at a composition location, while its exact storage and identity rules are SwiftUI's.

import SwiftUI

struct LocalToggle: View {
    @State private var expanded = false

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            Button(expanded ? "Collapse" : "Expand") {
                expanded.toggle()
            }
            if expanded {
                Text("Synthetic appointment details")
            }
        }
    }
}

The conditional operator condition ? a : b selects the button title. A trailing closure after Button supplies its action. toggle() mutates the Boolean. if within the builder conditionally describes a child; it does not imperatively hide a retained Android view. A change to expanded allows SwiftUI to update the relevant description.

Identity comes from the hierarchy and can be augmented explicitly. Moving between conditional branches or changing .id(value) can replace an identity and reset state. A random ID generated on every render creates accidental resets. An intentional new ID is appropriate when the product requests a fresh flow, as the picker demo does when showing the picker again. State is not process-death restoration or disk storage. It does not turn a draft into persistent data and may be destroyed when its owning identity leaves the hierarchy.

sections.title: A Binding is access to somebody else's source of truth
sections.html:
Passing a String gives a child a value to display. Passing a Binding<String> gives it read and write access to a source owned elsewhere. Angle brackets provide the generic type argument. A @Binding child property uses that access without creating a new independent state store. The projected value syntax $name produces a binding from a state wrapper; the dollar sign is wrapper projection, not string interpolation.

import SwiftUI

struct NameField: View {
    @Binding var name: String

    var body: some View {
        TextField("Demo name", text: $name)
    }
}

struct NameScreen: View {
    @State private var name = ""

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            NameField(name: $name)
            Text(name.isEmpty ? "No name yet" : name)
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

TextField's text: argument expects a binding because typing changes the value. NameField(name: $name) connects the child's generated initializer to the parent's storage. In Compose, the familiar counterpart is passing value = name plus onValueChange = { name = it }. SwiftUI packages those read/write operations into a binding. It does not imply a network write or domain validation.

A constant binding can preview a control but cannot accept edits into a changing source. A custom binding can transform input in its setter, but transformation can affect cursor position and should be intentional. Avoid duplicating the same draft into parent state and child state and synchronizing them with multiple change callbacks. That creates two sources of truth and difficult ordering rules; choose a single owner and derive the presentation.

sections.title: Observable models and Bindable editors
sections.html:
Observation supports reference models whose property accesses SwiftUI can track. @Observable is a macro that generates observation support at compile time. It is different from the @State property wrapper. With SwiftUI's Observation integration, a view depends on the observable properties it reads while computing its body, including reads reached through computed properties. Reading a model is enough to establish those dependencies; the model does not have to be locally owned by that view.

Observation-based SwiftUI APIs in this example require iOS 17 or later and a toolchain supporting the macro. The demo target declares iOS 18.2, so that deployment setting can use them. A deployment target answers which OS versions can run the target; a Swift language mode answers how the compiler interprets language rules. They are different settings. Applying @MainActor separately declares the model's isolation; observation itself does not make arbitrary concurrent mutation safe.

import Foundation
import Observation
import SwiftUI

@MainActor
@Observable
final class DemoDraft {
    var name = ""
    var acceptsReminder = false

    var canContinue: Bool {
        !name.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines).isEmpty
    }
}

@MainActor
struct DraftEditor: View {
    @Bindable var draft: DemoDraft

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            TextField("Demo name", text: $draft.name)
            Toggle("Reminder", isOn: $draft.acceptsReminder)
            Text(draft.canContinue ? "Ready" : "Enter a name")
        }
    }
}

@MainActor
struct DraftScreen: View {
    @State private var draft = DemoDraft()

    var body: some View {
        DraftEditor(draft: draft)
    }
}

@Bindable provides projections such as $draft.name for an observable object passed into an editor. It is not a request for persistence or a new ownership scope. The screen uses @State to maintain the locally created model reference across its identity. The computed canContinue reads name, so its display responds to name edits without storing an additional validity Boolean.

sections.title: Observation, ownership, and persistence answer different questions
sections.html:
Ask three separate questions. Observation asks which property changes should update the UI. Ownership asks which component keeps the model instance alive and decides when to replace it. Persistence asks how data survives destruction of the process or its in-memory owner. @Observable answers the first question. It does not automatically retain a delegate, cancel a task, save a draft, restore navigation, or survive logout. @State supplies identity-associated local storage; that still does not answer persistence.

A parent can create one observable model and pass it as a plain property to a read-only child. Use @Bindable when that child needs bindings for controls. The environment can distribute a dependency through a hierarchy, but distribution does not automatically define its business lifetime. An app-owned model may intentionally outlive individual screens; a form-owned model may be discarded when its flow finishes. Make those choices explicit instead of choosing wrappers by matching the word ViewModel from Android.

One subtle trap is initializing state from an input and expecting subsequent input changes to overwrite it. An initializer seeds the state for a new identity. If the parent later supplies a different record while the identity remains, existing draft state may remain. That may protect unsaved edits, or it may display the wrong record. Decide whether to reset identity, implement an explicit replace operation, or make the parent own the draft. Avoid side effects in model initialization because candidate instances can be created during description construction even when SwiftUI retains existing state storage.

sections.title: Legacy ObservableObject remains part of this codebase
sections.html:
The member-ID model conforms to ObservableObject and marks its changing state @Published. These belong to the older Combine-backed observation style. A view that creates and maintains such a model commonly uses @StateObject; a view receiving it commonly uses @ObservedObject. Both wrappers retain a reference, but @ObservedObject does not establish a stable owner-created instance across description reconstruction in the way @StateObject does.

Do not mechanically put @StateObject around an arbitrary class or @ObservedObject around a model using only Observation. The wrappers have protocol requirements. With an Observation-only model, use @State for local ownership and a plain reference or @Bindable for consumers. Incremental coexistence is normal: read the declared model type and the actual boundary before choosing a wrapper. Migrating a wrapper while leaving the model's protocol and notifications unchanged is not a complete migration.

The demo's MemberIdViewModelDemo receives its model and uses @ObservedObject; AddressFormDemo creates an observable address model in @State. These are concrete, current patterns, not evidence that every feature already uses one system. When reviewing a proposed migration, examine tests, publishers, delegate behavior, platform availability, and the owner of the instance. A smaller observation mechanism does not justify silently changing any of those contracts.

sections.title: Follow an edit through the active address form
sections.html:
Begin at the address demo's @State declaration, then inspect BookingAddressFormView's @Bindable model. A text field binds to a property such as street. The model's didSet property observer compares against oldValue, applies its constraints, and notifies a weak delegate. The computed currentAddress creates a value for consumers. That value is a projection of the current draft, not an automatic persisted record.

Notice display(address:) temporarily suppresses delegate notifications while populating fields. Programmatic prefill and user typing therefore have distinct event semantics even though both assign properties. setError skips identical assignments, which is useful when a controller evaluates form validity repeatedly. Read these decisions as part of the feature's public contract; an isolated SwiftUI tutorial that binds text directly to a plain String would not cover them.

Lastly, the demo retains its delegate coordinator in state because the model's delegate is weak. The coordinator also uses an observation annotation, but retention is supplied by the screen's state storage, not by the macro. This is the distinction to carry into future reviews: a screen that updates correctly can still lose callbacks or drafts if ownership is wrong.

quiz.question: What does @Observable guarantee for a model?
options: Its values are saved after process termination.
Its task lifetime matches an Android ViewModel.
Its property accesses and mutations can participate in observation.
quiz.explanation: The macro provides observation support. Owners still choose the model lifetime, synchronization, cancellation, and persistence strategy.

quiz.question: A child edits a parent's @State String. Which declaration expresses that relationship?
options: @Binding var name: String
@State private var name copied from the parent
let name: String
quiz.explanation: Binding supplies read/write access to the parent's source. A new State copy creates independent storage, while a plain immutable value cannot edit the original.

quiz.question: Why can changing .id(...) reset a form draft?
options: An ID writes an empty draft to disk.
It changes view identity, so SwiftUI can create fresh associated state.
IDs are only visual accessibility labels.
quiz.explanation: State is associated with identity. Explicit identity replacement can discard old storage. Accessibility identifiers are a different API and serve a different purpose.

exercise.brief: Create an observable synthetic draft owned by one scratch SwiftUI screen. Add an editable child and a read-only summary, then demonstrate deliberate identity reset.
steps: In a separate iOS 17+ learning target, implement DemoDraft, DraftScreen, and DraftEditor from the example.
Add a summary child with a plain DemoDraft property and read name and canContinue in its body.
Type a name, toggle the reminder, and force an unrelated parent state update. Explain why the draft stays.
Wrap the whole DraftScreen in a parent with @State resetKey = 0; apply .id(resetKey) and increment it through a Reset button.
Compare the address demo's wrappers with the member-ID demo; write the ownership and persistence answer for each.
acceptance: The editor and summary share one model reference and respond to name edits.
Unrelated parent updates preserve the draft while identity is stable.
A deliberate identity change creates fresh draft state.
The explanation explicitly separates observation, model ownership, and persistence.
exercise.solution:
A read-only child needs no binding wrapper when its body reads observable properties. It receives the same reference and observes those reads. The owner-created instance remains in the screen's state storage while its identity remains stable.

@MainActor
struct DraftSummary: View {
    let draft: DemoDraft
    var body: some View {
        Text(draft.canContinue ? draft.name : "Incomplete")
    }
}

@MainActor
struct ResettableDraft: View {
    @State private var resetKey = 0
    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            DraftScreen().id(resetKey)
            Button("Reset draft") { resetKey += 1 }
        }
    }
}

Add DraftSummary(draft: draft) beside the editor in DraftScreen. The parent key is an Int inferred from zero; changing it deliberately replaces the child identity. You should observe a new empty name and false reminder after Reset. This behavior is a product choice, so a production app should consider unsaved-edit confirmation separately. Both demo models here are in-memory; no wrapper promises disk restoration. The address model uses Observation plus State ownership, while the member-ID consumer observes an externally supplied ObservableObject. The latter boundary must be traced to its supplying owner rather than inferred from the word Observed.

lessons.title: Navigation and UIKit–SwiftUI interoperability
lessons.summary: Model route state and terminal results, bridge UI frameworks in both directions, and reason about coordinator lifetime and dismissal.
objectives: Represent navigation as routes or explicit UIKit flow operations.
Implement the make/update responsibilities of a representable bridge.
Host SwiftUI in UIKit without breaking controller containment.
Trace selection, back navigation, interactive dismissal, and flow completion in the picker.

sections.title: Navigation is a feature boundary, not just an animation
sections.html:
An Android feature often opens a destination and returns a selection or cancellation to its caller. Preserve that product-level thinking on iOS. A push changes a navigation stack; a modal presents a separate flow; dismissing a presentation and returning a result are related but distinct operations. The owning feature must decide which outcome completes the business interaction. A cancelled interactive transition must not accidentally report a completed selection.

UINavigationController manages UIKit controllers through operations such as pushViewController(_:animated:) and popViewController(animated:). SwiftUI's NavigationStack describes a root and destinations, optionally controlled by a bound path. Its analogy to Android's navigation back stack is useful, but it is not an interchangeable runtime. A UIKit coordinator can own navigation for SwiftUI content hosted inside a controller, so the existence of a SwiftUI view does not prove that a SwiftUI stack owns its flow.

Keep the outcome independent of visual details. A synthetic picker can return selected(id:) or cancelled while its owner chooses push versus modal presentation. The active visit-reason feature follows that separation. Its public coordinator exposes a result; the view and model remain internal. This gives callers a smaller integration contract than importing and manipulating every screen component.

sections.title: Typed routes and explicit path state
sections.html:
For a small SwiftUI flow, use a homogeneous route array. Hashable provides stable hashing and equality for route values, and Swift synthesizes conformance when associated data supports it. [Route] means an array of Route. Route.self is the type value passed to destination registration, not an instance of a route. case .detail(let id) extracts an enum's associated value.

import SwiftUI

enum DemoRoute: Hashable {
    case detail(id: String)
}

struct RouteDemo: View {
    @State private var path: [DemoRoute] = []

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List {
                NavigationLink("Open synthetic detail",
                               value: DemoRoute.detail(id: "demo-1"))
            }
            .navigationTitle("Demo")
            .navigationDestination(for: DemoRoute.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id):
                    VStack {
                        Text("Detail: \(id)")
                        Button("Return to root") { path.removeAll() }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

The link appends a route value; the destination registration maps that type to a description. Clearing the array returns to root. The binding makes path changes visible to the owner, including back navigation. Prefer stable identifiers over entire mutable record objects so routes do not silently change identity as the record changes. A route path is not automatic persistence; restoring it requires a deliberate encoding and validation policy. Heterogeneous NavigationPath is available, but a typed array is simpler when a feature has one route enum. These NavigationStack APIs require iOS 16 or later.

sections.title: Modal state and a precisely scoped dismiss action
sections.html:
SwiftUI's .sheet(isPresented:) associates a modal with a Boolean binding. .sheet(item:) associates it with an optional identifiable value. The item form makes the selected content and the presentation decision share one source. Identifiable requires an id representing stable identity; using the title as identity is unsafe when titles can change or collide.

@Environment(\.dismiss) reads a dismissal action from the current environment. The backslash-dot syntax is a key path identifying the environment value. Read it inside the sheet or destination that should dismiss. Reading the root's dismiss action and passing it into a sheet can target the wrong presentation context. Calling the action requests dismissal; it is not an automatic domain result or guarantee that a previous animation has completed.

Use explicit callbacks or a result type to report what happened. If a sheet supports swipe-to-dismiss, reconcile that path with the Cancel button. Decide whether unsaved edits should be preserved, discarded, or require confirmation. Programmatic selection and interactive dismissal can converge on an idempotent finish operation: the first terminal outcome wins, later duplicate callbacks do nothing. Idempotence prevents duplicate result delivery but does not excuse missing cleanup.

In UIKit, check which controller presents the modal and which one is dismissed. A modal navigation controller creates a distinct navigation hierarchy; its dismiss action is different from popping a pushed child. Also distinguish result timing from animation timing: a caller that immediately presents another screen may need to await or coordinate the transition. The active picker documents why its current modal caller can accept an immediate result.

sections.title: UIKit inside SwiftUI: creation and updates are different jobs
sections.html:
UIViewControllerRepresentable adapts a UIKit controller into a SwiftUI description. makeUIViewController(context:) creates the controller for a represented identity. updateUIViewController(_:context:) applies changing inputs to that existing controller. Context is a framework-provided type containing integration information, including the optional coordinator. SwiftUI calls these methods; they are not methods you call from body to force an update.

import SwiftUI
import UIKit

@MainActor
final class MessageController: UIViewController {
    private let label = UILabel()

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()
        view.backgroundColor = .systemBackground
        label.numberOfLines = 0
        label.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false
        view.addSubview(label)
        NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
            label.centerYAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.centerYAnchor),
            label.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.leadingAnchor, constant: 16),
            label.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.trailingAnchor, constant: -16)
        ])
    }

    func display(_ message: String) {
        loadViewIfNeeded()
        label.text = message
    }
}

@MainActor
struct UIKitMessage: UIViewControllerRepresentable {
    let message: String

    func makeUIViewController(context: Context) -> MessageController {
        MessageController()
    }

    func updateUIViewController(_ controller: MessageController, context: Context) {
        controller.display(message)
    }
}

The underscore before message removes its external label; call display(message). Loading the hierarchy before touching its label makes the update safe even if SwiftUI has not displayed it yet. The wrapper can be used as UIKitMessage(message: currentText) inside a SwiftUI container. It does not create a new controller for every text update. Empty update methods are suitable for static construction inputs, as in the demo's static UIKit screens, but will ignore later input changes if reused as dynamic components.

sections.title: Bridge callbacks with a stable coordinator
sections.html:
A representable's Coordinator is a class used to carry callback and delegate integration across ephemeral wrapper descriptions. makeCoordinator() creates it, and context.coordinator exposes it in make and update methods. It is an interoperability object, not automatically the same architectural abstraction as the feature's navigation coordinator. The identical name covers two different jobs.

For a text-field bridge, the coordinator commonly receives UIKit delegate changes and writes into a binding. Update the coordinator's current inputs in the update method rather than permanently capturing the first wrapper value. Otherwise a callback can call an obsolete closure or write to an obsolete binding. Before assigning text in an update, compare the existing value to avoid unnecessary selection or first-responder disruption. Do not emit a user-edit event merely because SwiftUI applied the same state again.

Subscriptions and callback lifetimes need equally explicit handling. The member-ID UIViewRepresentable stores Combine cancellables on its bridge coordinator. This keeps subscriptions alive for the integration's lifetime. A teardown hook such as dismantleUIViewController(_:coordinator:) can detach delegates or cancel work owned specifically by the wrapper, but it must not cancel a shared operation owned by another feature. Document ownership instead of using teardown as a blanket cleanup function.

A wrapper can also retain a feature coordinator through its UIKit host, as the picker demo does. That coordinator starts an asynchronous result flow. Avoid adding another nested navigation controller simply because the content is UIKit: first establish whether the surrounding destination already has a suitable navigation container.

sections.title: SwiftUI inside UIKit: hosting preserves ownership decisions
sections.html:
UIHostingController(rootView:) creates a UIKit controller from a SwiftUI description. UIKit can push it, present it, or contain it as a child. This lets a UIKit flow render a new SwiftUI component without rewriting navigation. If UIKit already owns the stack, a hosted child usually does not need another NavigationStack just to draw a title; navigation configuration belongs to the actual owning container.

Containment still requires addChild, installing and constraining the root view, and didMove(toParent:), as session 008 demonstrated. Keeping only the hosting controller's view while discarding its controller breaks that contract. For a table or collection cell, UIHostingConfiguration is a separate integration option with its own deployment requirements, not a substitute for every child-controller boundary.

The repository provides HostingController and HostingController_iOS16 helpers in its infrastructure. Those are project APIs, not Apple type names. Read their implementations when their extra behavior matters. The booking address model's bind() returns a hosting controller and configures safe-area treatment for its particular scroll-view integration. Do not copy safeAreaRegions = [] into every hosted screen: removing safe-area participation everywhere can put content beneath system UI. The containment and layout contract should describe the actual parent.

sections.title: Follow every picker exit, including the user's gesture
sections.html:
Read the demo host's viewDidAppear guard: it needs an existing navigation controller and starts only once per retained coordinator. Follow didStart() in the active coordinator. It validates nonempty input, constructs and retains its model, assigns itself as weak delegate, hosts the SwiftUI picker, and chooses pushed or modal presentation. The host's retained coordinator keeps the flow alive; Observation on the model does not.

Selection reaches the model's delegate and then the coordinator's result path. A pushed flow pops; a modal flow dismisses. The pushed host observes removal from its parent, while a retained UIAdaptivePresentationControllerDelegate adapter observes interactive modal dismissal. The adapter must be retained because the presentation controller's delegate reference does not supply its lifetime. Both explicit cancellation and selection also cancel optional fetch work.

The empty-input demo is a deliberately invalid invocation, not the ordinary search-no-results state. The coordinator reports a runtime bug, presents a generic alert, and completes with cancellation after the alert is dismissed. Search-no-results instead remains an active picker with input the user can change. Keeping those cases distinct avoids shipping a dead-end feature disguised as an empty list.

quiz.question: A hosted SwiftUI picker is pushed by UINavigationController. Who owns that navigation stack?
options: The picker automatically owns a NavigationStack.
The UINavigationController and the flow owner that operates it.
The model's Observable macro.
quiz.explanation: SwiftUI rendering does not change the stack's owner. UIKit still retains and transitions its controller stack; the coordinator controls the feature's operations.

quiz.question: Why update the bridge coordinator's callback in updateUIViewController?
options: To keep it aligned with the latest representable inputs.
To recreate the entire UIKit controller after each edit.
To make callbacks persist after process death.
quiz.explanation: Wrapper values can be recreated while the bridge coordinator remains stable. An old callback capture can target stale inputs unless the current integration state is refreshed.

quiz.question: What is the distinction between an empty initial procedure array and an unsuccessful search?
options: Both always finish the flow as cancelled.
Only an unsuccessful search can produce a runtime error.
Invalid initial input makes selection impossible; search-no-results is a reversible UI state.
quiz.explanation: The active coordinator guards invalid empty initialization. Search remains within a valid flow, and the user can edit the query to find supported choices.

lessons.title: Async first steps: suspension, cancellation, and UI state
lessons.summary: Call asynchronous Swift APIs safely from a screen, make cancellation cooperative, and prevent obsolete responses from winning a UI race.
objectives: Read async, throws, try await, Task, and cancellation checks accurately.
Distinguish view-associated tasks from manually created unstructured tasks.
Keep UI state on the main actor while treating await as a possible interleaving point.
Represent loading outcomes and reject stale responses with an explicit request policy.

sections.title: From suspend functions to Swift async functions
sections.html:
Consider an Android search screen: typing launches a coroutine, an HTTP operation suspends, and a newer query can make the earlier result obsolete. Swift has the same engineering problem. A function marked async may suspend while it waits; a caller uses await at a possible suspension point. throws permits failure, and try await handles both effects. This is conceptually similar to calling a Kotlin suspend function inside a coroutine, but the exact task hierarchy, isolation, and lifecycle integration need separate investigation.

await does not mean create a background thread. It does not promise a suspension every time, and it does not automatically parallelize two calls. Calling one async function and then another still expresses a sequence. Thread or executor behavior depends on actor isolation, the function's declaration, and toolchain settings. A heavy synchronous calculation in main-actor code can block the UI even if its enclosing function is async.

This lesson deliberately uses a main-actor synthetic service whose only waiting operation suspends. That avoids claiming a universal background execution rule. Later sessions cover structured child tasks, actors, Sendable, and executor behavior. For now, learn to mark each suspension point, identify the owner of the task, and decide whether the result still belongs to the current screen state when execution resumes.

sections.title: Read a small asynchronous operation
sections.html:
The following code is suitable for an iOS learning target or an async Swift harness with the relevant standard library and Foundation support. It performs no network request and uses only synthetic strings. enum DemoLoadError: Error defines an error value; throw exits with it. 200_000_000 is a numeric literal with readability separators, representing 200 million nanoseconds.

import Foundation

enum DemoLoadError: Error {
    case unavailable
}

@MainActor
struct DemoLoader {
    func load(for id: String) async throws -> String {
        try await Task.sleep(nanoseconds: 200_000_000)
        try Task.checkCancellation()
        if id == "fail" {
            throw DemoLoadError.unavailable
        }
        return "Synthetic result for \(id)"
    }
}

for is the external label, and id is the parameter's local name; call load(for: "demo-1"). The arrow specifies the successful return type. Task.sleep suspends the task rather than blocking a thread. It throws if cancellation interrupts the sleep. The additional cancellation check demonstrates checking the task's flag before publishing subsequent work, even though this particular sleep already responds to cancellation.

Modern toolchains also provide duration-based sleep overloads such as Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(200)). Check their platform availability before replacing a project's existing abstraction. In this checkout, the member-ID feature injects an AsyncSleep dependency, allowing tests to control timeout behavior. That repository protocol is an integration choice, not a new Swift keyword. Never replace suspension with a blocking Thread.sleep just to make an async example appear predictable.

sections.title: A task needs a lifetime owner
sections.html:
An async function can call another async function directly with await; that call remains part of the same task. A synchronous button callback cannot suspend, so Task { ... } creates an asynchronous task from that event. This task is unstructured: it does not become a lifecycle-managed child merely because the source line is inside a view. Its returned handle lets an owner await its result or request cancellation.

Task<Void, Never> describes a task returning no useful value and exposing no thrown error. Void is the empty tuple type; Never represents an impossible value, here indicating that the task closure handles its failures. Dropping the handle does not cancel the task. The task can retain objects captured by its closure, so deallocation is not a reliable stop mechanism.

SwiftUI's .task { ... } modifier supplies view-associated asynchronous work. .task(id: value) also requests cancellation and restarts when its Equatable ID changes. This is a useful conceptual neighbor of Compose's LaunchedEffect(key), but not a claim of identical implementation. SwiftUI can cancel work when the view disappears before it completes; the operation must still cooperate. Do not wrap the awaited operation in a nested Task inside the modifier: that creates a separate unstructured task and can lose the cancellation relationship you expected.

A UIKit coordinator instead may store a task property and cancel it on the flow's explicit finish path. Choose the owner according to whether work belongs to a visible screen, an entire feature flow, or a shared service.

sections.title: Cancellation is a request with a contract
sections.html:
handle.cancel() sets cancellation state and notifies cancellation handlers. It does not forcibly kill a thread or guarantee that arbitrary code stops immediately. Cooperative APIs may throw CancellationError; your own code can call Task.checkCancellation() to throw when cancelled, or inspect Task.isCancelled to take a nonthrowing branch. Checking only before a long operation is insufficient if the user leaves while the operation is suspended.

Cancellation usually is not a user-facing service failure. A screen disappearing, a newer search replacing an older one, or a user choosing manual entry are normal reasons to stop. However, an API can use its own error type for cancellation: networking may report a cancelled URL error rather than Swift's CancellationError. Use the task flag plus the service's documented error behavior when classifying failures. Do not assume one catch clause recognizes every cancellation source.

Cancellation also is not freshness. A service might ignore cancellation or finish just before it receives the request. If an old response can race with a newer one, check a request token or revision before changing shared UI state. That check is necessary even when all model properties are main-actor isolated. Actor isolation prevents concurrent unsynchronized access; it does not preserve a pre-await assumption across suspension.

Avoid swallowing errors with try? and then continuing as if work succeeded. That converts both failure and cancellation into an optional and can publish misleading defaults. Prefer an explicit do/catch whose branches express the intended UI outcomes.

sections.title: An explicit loading state with a freshness guard
sections.html:
Use one enum instead of unrelated loading, error, and result flags that can contradict each other. In this iOS 17+ example, @Observable enables view updates, @MainActor isolates the model, and private(set) allows public reading within the model's visibility while restricting assignment to its implementation. A revision increments for each load, so every suspended operation knows which request it belongs to.

import Observation

@MainActor
@Observable
final class DemoLoadingModel {
    enum Phase: Equatable {
        case idle
        case loading
        case loaded(String)
        case failed(String)
    }

    private(set) var phase: Phase = .idle
    private var revision = 0

    func load(id: String) async {
        revision += 1
        let requestRevision = revision
        phase = .loading
        do {
            let message = try await DemoLoader().load(for: id)
            try Task.checkCancellation()
            guard requestRevision == revision else { return }
            phase = .loaded(message)
        } catch {
            guard requestRevision == revision else { return }
            if Task.isCancelled || error is CancellationError {
                phase = .idle
            } else {
                phase = .failed("Unable to load the synthetic result")
            }
        }
    }
}

do groups throwing operations. A general catch exposes its error as error. is tests an error's runtime type; || is logical OR. The freshness guard runs in both success and failure paths, so an old cancellation cannot clear a newer result. This small model treats cancellation of the latest request as idle. Another product might retain previously loaded data; choose and test that policy rather than deriving it from the async keyword.

sections.title: Call the model in the view's task
sections.html:
This view belongs in an iOS 17+ SwiftUI target alongside the preceding model and service. The owner stores the observable model in State. The input id is a plain value supplied by a parent; changing it restarts the modifier's work for the current identity. The switch is exhaustive, so each representable phase has a rendering.

import SwiftUI

@MainActor
struct DemoLoadingScreen: View {
    let id: String
    @State private var model = DemoLoadingModel()

    var body: some View {
        Group {
            switch model.phase {
            case .idle:
                Text("Ready")
            case .loading:
                ProgressView("Loading")
            case .loaded(let message):
                Text(message)
            case .failed(let message):
                Text(message)
            }
        }
        .task(id: id) {
            await model.load(id: id)
        }
    }
}

Group combines descriptions without choosing a stack layout. ProgressView is a framework control for progress feedback. The associated-value let message binds the payload for its case. The task directly awaits the model method and therefore observes cancellation in that task. The revision policy protects against overlapping requests during rapid input changes.

For a retry button, either change a retry token included in the task ID or retain a deliberately managed Task handle. A button whose only action creates an untracked Task may still be fine for short, intentional flow work, but its ownership policy should be explicit. A retry key that changes every render is a bug: it turns updates into a perpetual restart loop.

sections.title: Read current cancellation behavior without promising more
sections.html:
In PrefillMemberIdViewModel, starting a load creates separate fetching and timeout tasks. Choosing manual entry calls a reset method that cancels pending tasks and changes the state. After fetching, the implementation checks cancellation before publishing its result and confirms it is still loading. That explains how the user's explicit choice can win over a delayed response. Its timeout and sleep dependency make deterministic testing possible.

The visit-reason coordinator owns an optional fetch task for common suggestions. A failed fetch degrades to an empty optional section while the full supported procedure list remains usable. Before changing the model after suspension, it checks Task.isCancelled. That policy differs from the primary member-ID retrieval, whose failure changes a central form state. Error handling must reflect the role of the data.

Do not infer that every callback-launched Task in the demos has full cancellation handling; the age-warning demo uses a task to await an alert result without storing a handle. Demos can illustrate integration with narrower lifetime assumptions. A production review should identify its owner, stopping event, result relevance, and tests before adopting the pattern elsewhere.

quiz.question: What does await guarantee about execution?
options: The caller runs on a new background thread.
The operation can suspend; actor and executor rules still determine execution context.
The awaited operation runs in parallel with every following line.
quiz.explanation: Await marks a possible suspension point. It neither creates a thread nor parallelizes a sequence, and main-actor synchronous work can still block rendering.

quiz.question: Why use a revision check after await even when a previous task was cancelled?
options: Cancellation cannot be requested from the main actor.
The service may finish despite cancellation, and the response can be obsolete.
Observable models cannot store enums.
quiz.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative, and an older result may race with replacement. A revision check implements freshness independently of the service's cancellation behavior.

quiz.question: Which call preserves a SwiftUI task modifier's cancellation context?
options: .task { await model.load(id: id) }
.task { Task { await model.load(id: id) } }
Button action with an unretained Task always cancels on disappearance.
quiz.explanation: Directly awaiting the operation keeps it in the modifier's task. A nested Task creates unstructured work whose lifetime is not automatically the same.

exercise.solution:
Suppose A starts with revision 1 and B starts with revision 2 while A is suspended. If A succeeds later, its revision comparison fails, so it returns without publishing. If A fails or is cancelled, the catch-path comparison also fails, so it cannot reset B's state. B alone may publish loaded, failed, or idle according to its own outcome.

For deterministic model reasoning, replace the delay with a controlled fake in your own scratch target so you can complete B before A. A direct service dependency makes this easy: inject a main-actor async throwing closure or protocol rather than depending on wall-clock timing. Do not claim the rapid-tap manual experiment proves all schedules; it only demonstrates one observed run.

When the current screen's task is cancelled, the model checks the task flag or CancellationError and uses its chosen idle policy. A production form could preserve prior data instead. The member-ID feature specifically resets to manual entry because that is the user's action, and its post-fetch cancellation check protects that decision. The important result is a documented transition policy plus a freshness guard, not a particular spinner or timeout duration.

lessons.title: XCTest, Swift Testing, UI automation, and snapshots
lessons.summary: Choose a test boundary, write expressive assertions, control async behavior, and review visual baselines without confusing snapshots with correctness.
objectives: Write equivalent behavior tests using XCTest and Swift Testing.
Explain test discovery, optional assertions, actor isolation, and parallel-test hazards.
Test cancellation with controlled completion rather than arbitrary sleeps.
Distinguish unit, integration, snapshot, and UI-automation evidence in the active demo.

sections.title: Start with the behavior you want evidence for
sections.html:
Your Android testing instincts transfer well: isolate decisions, fake external dependencies, and reserve expensive device automation for integration paths that require it. On iOS, XCTest supports unit tests, performance tests, and UI automation through XCUIAutomation. Swift Testing is a newer Swift-native unit-testing framework included with Xcode 16 and later. They can coexist in a project or target; use the assertion and lifecycle APIs appropriate to the framework of each test rather than mixing them inside one test.

A pure query-normalization test proves how a function handles strings. A model test proves state transitions and delegate decisions. A coordinator integration test can verify a controller is pushed and a selection produces a result. A snapshot detects a visual change under configured rendering conditions. A UI test launches an app and interacts with its accessibility-exposed elements. None subsumes all the others.

Write the evidence you need before choosing a framework. For the picker, whitespace trimming belongs in a fast model test; search-no-results presentation belongs in a snapshot or UI assertion; swipe-back cancellation belongs near the coordinator or actual navigation integration. A screenshot of a list cannot prove that its selection reaches the caller exactly once. Conversely, a correct selected-ID assertion cannot prove that a long localized label is readable.

sections.title: XCTest discovery and precise assertions
sections.html:
import XCTest exposes the framework. A test class subclasses XCTestCase, and test methods conventionally start with test. final prevents subclassing but is not the discovery mechanism. XCTAssertEqual compares values and records a test failure rather than throwing a Swift error. The helper below is synthetic, and both it and the test belong in a learner's testable module and test target.

import Foundation

func demoFilteredNames(_ names: [String], query: String) -> [String] {
    let normalized = query.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
    guard !normalized.isEmpty else { return names }
    return names.filter { $0.localizedCaseInsensitiveContains(normalized) }
}
import XCTest

final class DemoFilterTests: XCTestCase {
    func testTrailingWhitespaceStillMatches() {
        let names = ["Demo Dental", "Demo Eye"]
        let result = demoFilteredNames(names, query: "dental ")
        XCTAssertEqual(result, ["Demo Dental"])
    }

    func testWhitespaceOnlyReturnsOriginalChoices() {
        let names = ["Demo Dental", "Demo Eye"]
        XCTAssertEqual(demoFilteredNames(names, query: "   "), names)
    }
}

$0 is the first implicit closure parameter, here a candidate string. The query: argument label makes the call's purpose clear. An array equality assertion checks both membership and order, which is stronger than checking only the count. @testable import ModuleName grants a test target access to internal declarations of a module built with testability enabled; it does not expose private implementation or magically import app resources.

When a result is optional, prefer try XCTUnwrap(value) in a throwing test method. It records a failure and stops that path if the value is nil. Force unwraps can crash the test host and obscure the intended assertion. Avoid reproducing the entire production algorithm in the test's expected-value calculation; use a small, independently understood fixture.

sections.title: Swift Testing attributes, macros, and parameters
sections.html:
Swift Testing discovers @Test-annotated functions; a function does not need a test-name prefix. @Suite optionally names or configures a suite. A struct can group tests without subclassing XCTestCase. The hash-prefixed #expect and #require are macros that expand assertions with useful expression diagnostics. An expectation records a failed check and continues; a requirement throws if the required condition or optional unwrap fails.

import Testing

@Suite("Synthetic query matching")
struct DemoQueryTests {
    @Test("Case and surrounding whitespace are ignored",
          arguments: ["dental", "DENTAL", " dental "])
    func findsDental(query: String) {
        let result = demoFilteredNames(["Demo Dental", "Demo Eye"], query: query)
        #expect(result == ["Demo Dental"])
    }

    @Test("Missing matches produce an empty array")
    func hasNoResults() {
        #expect(demoFilteredNames(["Demo Dental"], query: "zzz").isEmpty)
    }

    @Test("First match has a readable name")
    func unwrapsFirstMatch() throws {
        let result = demoFilteredNames(["Demo Dental"], query: "dental")
        let first = try #require(result.first)
        #expect(first == "Demo Dental")
    }
}

arguments: runs the same behavior check for each supplied value, passing it to the function parameter. result.first is optional because an array may be empty; the requirement establishes the precondition for the next check. This is a useful conceptual counterpart to parameterized JUnit tests, with framework-specific discovery and failure semantics.

Swift Testing commonly runs tests in parallel. New suite instances isolate instance properties, but globals, singleton dependencies, UserDefaults domains, font registration, and shared files can still collide. A serialized suite trait can be appropriate for a narrowly justified shared resource, but it is not a replacement for isolated test fixtures. Main-actor annotations control UI access, not the isolation of all business state shared between tests.

sections.title: Async tests should await evidence, not elapsed time
sections.html:
Both frameworks support async test functions. Add @MainActor when constructing or calling a main-actor model or UIKit object; do not assume all test methods execute there. When an async operation directly returns the result, await it and assert that result. For callback APIs, XCTest expectations and asynchronous fulfillment provide bounded waiting. Avoid a blocking wait on the main actor when fulfillment requires that same actor.

A meaningful cancellation test first arranges the operation, then requests cancellation, awaits task completion, and checks the defined outcome. The next Swift Testing example uses the model and service from session 011 in the same scratch module. It tests pre-cancelled work rather than a transport race:

import Testing

@Test("Cancelled load returns to idle")
@MainActor
func cancelledLoadIsIdle() async {
    let model = DemoLoadingModel()
    let operation = Task { await model.load(id: "demo-1") }
    operation.cancel()
    await operation.value
    #expect(model.phase == .idle)
}

operation.value awaits completion; because this task handles errors internally, the await does not need try. To test cancellation after an operation begins, inject a fake service with a start signal and controlled completion. Await the start signal, cancel, then release or complete the fake. A Task.yield() or a short sleep does not prove the fake reached a particular stage.

For stale-response behavior, start A, wait until the fake records A, start B, complete B, then complete A. Assert B's result stays. Also test an old failure. The checkout's member-ID configuration injects AsyncSleep for timeout control. That seam is more reliable than increasing a timeout until a flaky test happens to pass on one machine.

sections.title: Snapshots are reviewed visual contracts
sections.html:
SnapshotTesting is a third-party library used by this repository. It is not Apple's XCTest assertion API. The local assertStandardSnapshot(of:) helper wraps it with fixed dimensions, safe-area insets, light appearance, display scale, font registration, and configured comparison precision. The exact environment still matters: OS font rendering, SDK changes, layout timing, and animation can cause diffs even when those local traits are fixed.

A snapshot must render a deterministic state. Use a synthetic fixture and explicitly set loading, loaded, failure, or no-results before capture. Wait for the intended layout or disable nonessential animation through the project's established mechanism. Do not snapshot a live network request or the wall-clock phase of a shimmer and then pretend that image is stable. The demo's picker snapshots construct default, filtered, and no-results states through demo hooks.

Recording is a review operation, not a way to make assertions pass. When a diff appears, inspect the previous baseline, the new image, and the reason for the change. Confirm that fonts registered correctly, the expected state was loaded, and the rendering environment matches. Re-record only an understood intended change. The helper reads a recording environment variable, but enabling it blindly can overwrite accepted visual evidence.

One standard phone-size baseline does not establish accessibility, large-text, dark-mode, localization, or tablet correctness. Add targeted evidence for changes that affect those behaviors. A tolerance can absorb small rendering noise; it can also hide a small regression. Choose its meaning deliberately instead of raising precision thresholds until review disappears.

sections.title: UI automation operates across the app boundary
sections.html:
XCTest UI tests use XCUIApplication to launch and query the app under test. The test runner and app are separate execution contexts, so a plain test variable is not an app dependency injection seam. Configure deterministic app behavior through an explicit test launch contract or existing demo fixtures. Query by stable accessibility identifiers when possible; a visible label can change through localization or copy editing.

import XCTest

final class ScratchDemoUITests: XCTestCase {
    func testSyntheticDetailCanOpen() {
        let app = XCUIApplication()
        app.launch()
        let open = app.buttons["Open synthetic detail"]
        XCTAssertTrue(open.waitForExistence(timeout: 3))
        open.tap()
        XCTAssertTrue(app.staticTexts["Detail: demo-1"].waitForExistence(timeout: 3))
    }
}

This example requires a UI-test target attached to the session 010 scratch app, with the RouteDemo detail showing that text. It is not a runnable standalone Swift program. waitForExistence(timeout:) returns a Bool, which the assertion checks; ignoring that return can let a test continue without evidence. Query types must match what accessibility exposes: an apparent text block might be a text view rather than a static text.

The active empty-picker UI test demonstrates this distinction by querying the alert's description as a text view and checking the cancelled result after dismissal. That path proves integration the pure filtering tests cannot. Keep UI tests few and purposeful because app launch, animations, keyboard interaction, and simulator conditions make them slower and more variable than model checks.

sections.title: Use the checkout's test layers as a coverage map
sections.html:
Read a member-ID demo snapshot to identify its presentation fixture, then read the feature model tests to identify state and delegate assertions. Read the picker coordinator tests for selected and cancelled results and the Swift Testing tests in InsuranceHome for an actual modern suite. The codebase already contains both frameworks; teaching one as the only current convention would be misleading.

The demo Project.swift declares an app target, a unit-test target, and a UI-test target. Those declarations establish available integration boundaries, not evidence that tests were executed successfully. This course author inspected source and contracts; it did not run the client suite or regenerate any baselines. When you run your own checks, record the scheme, simulator runtime, fixture state, and result. Distinguish a compiler failure, an assertion failure, and a baseline-environment mismatch before making a change.

A useful review asks which requirement each test proves and what would fail if the requirement broke. If removing the normalization still passes your query test, your fixture is too forgiving. If disconnecting the selection callback still passes every screenshot, add result-level evidence. Strong tests expose behavior boundaries instead of mirroring implementation line by line.

quiz.question: A snapshot shows the selected row correctly. What remains unproven?
options: Whether the visual fixture changed under the configured renderer.
Whether the selection result reaches its caller exactly once.
Whether an image baseline exists.
quiz.explanation: A visual comparison observes rendering. Result delivery, lifetime, and duplicate completion need model or coordinator integration assertions.

quiz.question: In Swift Testing, when should you use try #require(optional)?
options: When later assertions require a non-nil value and the test should stop if it is missing.
Whenever you want to silently ignore a failed check.
To import private app properties into a UI test process.
quiz.explanation: Require records the failed requirement and throws when its optional cannot be unwrapped. Expect is suitable for independent checks that can continue.

quiz.question: Which strategy tests an A/B response race most reliably?
options: Sleep for one second after starting A and assume it began.
Raise the test timeout until CI passes.
Use a fake that signals start and lets the test complete B before A.
quiz.explanation: Controlled scheduling establishes the exact race under test. Timing guesses depend on machine load and do not prove the prerequisite stages occurred.

Those fixtures independently encode behavior. The pre-cancelled loading test should end at idle and await its operation, so no outstanding task can mutate state after the assertion.

For A/B completion, have the fake store one pending operation per synthetic request ID and notify the test when each has started. Complete B with its synthetic result and observe loaded B. Complete A with either a different result or an error and observe that loaded B remains. The test should fail if the model removes its success or catch freshness guard. Explicitly finish and clean up every pending fake operation so the test cannot hang.

A loaded and failed snapshot pair checks distinct visible contracts under a fixed environment, while a coordinator assertion checks the terminal selection payload. The demo's empty-input UI test checks the generic alert, dismisses it, and waits for Cancelled. That is evidence for invalid invocation recovery, not the same requirement as search-no-results rendering.
